name: Accommodation Alerts for Every Teacher
title: Accommodation Alerts for Every Teacher
answer: Accommodation alerts for every teacher means using student information systems and AI to give each teacher short, clear notes about the accommodations a student requires. It matters because a support like extended time only works when every teacher, including substitutes and elective teachers, knows to provide it. The alerts must protect privacy and arrive at useful moments, not just once at the start of the year.

sections.body: A student's accommodations only take effect when all the adults who teach that student know what to do. If a substitute, an elective teacher, or another staff member never sees the plan, the student may not receive the support in that class. Student information systems can alert teachers who have the student on their rosters. AI can help by turning long accommodation lists into short, clear notes for each teacher. This closes the gap between a written plan and what actually happens in classrooms.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give grade bands for this practice. In a school, alerts would go through the student information system to the teachers who have the student on their rosters, including substitutes and elective teachers. AI would help convert a long accommodation list into a brief note that tells each teacher what to do. Because a note at the start of the year is easily forgotten, reminders before tests and at the start of new units help. Case managers can check whether accommodations are being provided by asking teachers and students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for accommodation alerts. It describes a practical workflow and a follow-up role rather than reporting research results. On the text provided, this idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Accommodation information is private and should be shared only with staff who work with the student. The note should say what the teacher needs to do, not describe the student's disability in detail. A teacher needs to know that a student gets preferential seating and breaks, not the student's diagnosis. Timing is also a limit, since a single start-of-year note can be forgotten, so reminders before tests and new units matter. The alert is a tool, and the case manager's follow up is what makes it work.
